question: Your rover plans on a slippery floor with a pit. What does V(s) mean for a square s in the MDP?
options: The number of moves the rover needs to reach the goal from s
The reward you can expect from s if you play the best moves
The reward of the next move alone, averaged over slips
explanation: V(s) is the reward you can expect from square s onward, averaged over the slips, when the best moves are played. It is the reward-to-go of 13/03 averaged over chance.

question: You write one backup of V(s) for your slippery-floor rover. What does it compute for a square?
options: Reward now plus gamma times the next square's value, for the best move
Reward now plus the next square's value with no discount, for the best move
Reward now plus gamma times the next square's value, averaged over all moves
explanation: The backup scores each move by its reward now plus gamma times the next square's value, then keeps the best one. Taking the best move, not the average, makes it the best value.

question: Your rover's value iteration runs with gamma = 0.9. How much does one sweep shrink the worst-case error at most?
options: By a factor 0.1, one minus gamma
By a factor 0.9, equal to gamma
explanation: In one update the next square's value enters multiplied by gamma, so any error in it shrinks by gamma as well. With gamma at 0.9 the worst error becomes 0.9 times as big.

question: Your rover runs value iteration with 0 < gamma < 1, rewards of size at most 1 and V starting at 0. Why can any small error target be reached in a bounded number of sweeps?
options: Each sweep fixes one more square, so squares set the count
The greedy policy stops changing, so V is frozen from then on
Changes start at most 1 and shrink by gamma or less each sweep
explanation: Each sweep shrinks the change by gamma or less, and gamma is below one, so the changes drop below any small target after enough sweeps.

question: A pit sits beside your rover's short route and moves slip sideways. What does the greedy policy do at the start?
options: May pick a longer route that steers clear of the pit
Takes the short route, because fewer steps always win
Picks any route, since slips make them all equal
explanation: The chance of sliding into the pit costs an expected -1, which can be worse than the small discount a longer route pays, so the longer route can win.

question: You want value iteration for a new rover task. When can you not use it?
options: When moves slip, so the outcomes are left to chance
When several squares carry a negative reward
When you do not know the move chances and rewards
explanation: Each sweep needs the chance of every outcome and every reward. Without them you have to learn from tries instead, as in policy gradients.
